[princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp)
## This session

### 1) Base R plots ::: {.fragment fragment-index="1"} - Your first plots: scatter, line, histogram, bar, density - The canvas model: layering with `lines()`, `points()`, `abline()` - Many plots at once; maps :::
### 2) `ggplot2` ::: {.fragment fragment-index="2"} - Plots as objects, built from layers - Geoms, facets, scales, and labels - Making and saving publication-ready figures ::: ::: {.fragment fragment-index="3"}
Conclude with Quarto report exercise ::: ## Some sources

- Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund, *R for Data Science*, 2e - [Ch. 1: Data visualization](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize.html) - [Ch. 9: Layers](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/layers.html) - Harvard IQSS, *Math Prefresher for Political Scientists* - [Ch. 10: Visualization](https://iqss.github.io/prefresher/14_visualization.html) - `ggplot2` documentation - [Function reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/) — every geom, scale, and theme - [Aesthetic specifications](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html) — every point shape, line type, and color name # Base R plots ## Our data, again

The county data from yesterday — income and rent, plus population and region: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} counties <- left_join( read_csv("data/county_data.csv"), read_csv("data/county_population.csv"), join_by(GEOID == fips) ) ``` ::: ## Our data, again

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(counties) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 3,144 Columns: 10 $ GEOID "01001", "01003", "01005", "01007", "01009", "01011", "01… $ state "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "Alabama", "A… $ county "Autauga County", "Baldwin County", "Barbour County", "Bi… $ income 69841, 75019, 44290, 51215, 61096, 36723, 44881, 55826, 4… $ income_moe 5512, 2751, 2762, 6678, 3328, 6836, 4130, 2168, 5005, 489… $ rent 1200, 1211, 644, 802, 743, 635, 722, 804, 850, 750, 855, … $ rent_moe 75, 42, 41, 129, 27, 93, 17, 28, 61, 74, 65, 135, 104, 13… $ region "South", "South", "South", "South", "South", "South", "So… $ division "East South Central", "East South Central", "East South C… $ pop 58805, 231767, 25223, 22293, 59134, 10357, 19051, 116441,… ``` ::: ::: ## Your first plot

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(counties$income, counties$rent) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## A bunch of hidden defaults we can fill ourselves

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot( counties$income / 1000, counties$rent, main = "Rent vs. income", xlab = "Median household income (in thousands USD)", ylab = "Median gross rent", pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "steelblue" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=672} ::: ::: ## Useful plot arguments

| Argument | What it controls | Example | |:---------------|:-----------------------|:---------------------------| | `main` | title | `main = "Rent vs. income"` | | `xlab`, `ylab` | axis labels | `xlab = "Income"` | | `col` | color | `col = "steelblue"` | | `pch` | point shape | `pch = 19` (filled circle) | | `cex` | point size | `cex = 0.5` (half size) | | `type` | points vs. lines | `type = "l"` | | `lwd`, `lty` | line width, line style | `lwd = 2, lty = "dashed"` |
::: fragment The same arguments work across `plot()`, `lines()`, `points()`, `hist()`, and friends ::: ::: fragment Menus: [`?points`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/points.html) draws every `pch`, [`?par`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/graphics/html/par.html) covers the rest, `colors()` lists all 657 names ::: # ggplot2 ## From canvas to objects

Base R: call functions, ink appears on a device. The plot is a **side effect.** ::: fragment `ggplot2`: builds an object that describes a plot with layers. Gets drawn when you print it. :::
::: fragment That means you can assign, modify, combine, save, etc. _without printing anything_. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(...) # nothing drawn yet p # drawn now ``` ::: :::
::: fragment `ggplot2` is part of the tidyverse you met yesterday: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) ``` ::: ::: ## The gist: (data w/ mapping) + geom + ...

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment (Yuck.) ::: ## Aesthetics

Map a third column to color. It's a variable, so it goes in `aes()` (constants go in `geom_*`) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = region)) + geom_point(size = 0.7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment Compare: in base R, *you* subset the data, chose the colors, and drew the legend. ::: ## Classic mistake

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = "steelblue")) + geom_point(size = 0.7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment Inside `aes()`, `"steelblue"` isn't a color. It gets vectorized as data. ::: ## Same mapping, different geom

Distributions by group: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = region, y = income)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Composition: stacked bars

Split each region's counties into high- and low-population halves: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} counties <- counties |> mutate(pop_level = if_else( pop >= median(counties$pop, na.rm = T), "high pop", "low_pop" )) counties |> filter(!is.na(pop_level)) |> ## piping in this data; now different operator! ggplot(aes(x = region, fill = pop_level)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Counts vs. shares: `position`

`position = "fill"` rescales every bar to 1 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(!is.na(pop_level)) |> ggplot(aes(x = region, fill = pop_level)) + geom_bar(position = "fill") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Side by side: `position = "dodge"`

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(!is.na(pop_level)) |> ggplot(aes(x = region, fill = pop_level)) + geom_bar(position = "dodge") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment *Three versions of the same bars — stacked, filled, dodged. Which question does each answer best?* ::: ## Line graphs

`ggplot2` ships with practice data: `economics` is monthly US macro data: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Common mistake

::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(economics_long, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 4 date variable value value01 1 1967-07-01 pce 507. 0 2 1967-08-01 pce 510. 0.000265 3 1967-09-01 pce 516. 0.000762 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(economics_long, aes(x = date, y = value01)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: ## Tell ggplot what belongs together

Map the series id to `color` (or `group`) and each variable gets its own line: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(economics_long, aes(x = date, y = value01, color = variable)) + geom_line() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Reference lines are geoms too

::: fragment `geom_hline()`, `geom_vline()`, and `geom_abline()` are just more layers: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.5, color = "gray") + geom_hline( yintercept = median(counties$rent, na.rm = T), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: ## Facets

One line splits the plot by a categorical column: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~region) ## more than one: ~ region + ... ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Facets in two directions

`facet_grid(rows ~ cols)`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} counties |> filter(!is.na(pop_level)) |> ggplot(aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.4) + facet_grid(pop_level ~ region) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Labels with `labs()`

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = region)) + geom_point(size = 0.7) + labs( title = "Rent rises with income", subtitle = "US counties, 2023 five-year ACS", x = "Median household income ($)", y = "Median gross rent ($)", color = "Region" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Scales: _how_ mappings become positions and colors

Every aesthetic has a scale named `scale__()` with its own arguments: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.5) + scale_x_continuous( name = "Median household income", breaks = c(50000, 100000, 150000), labels = c("$50k", "$100k", "$150k"), limits = c(0, 200000) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Zooming vs. dropping

`xlim()`/`ylim()`/`lims()` **throw away data** outside the limits: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.5) + lims(x = c(0, 100000)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Removed 158 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Zooming vs. dropping

`coord_cartesian()` **zooms** without dropping: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent)) + geom_point(size = 0.5) + coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100000)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: :::: fragment ::: blocktext Looks the same here, but anything *computed* from the data (boxplot stats, smoothers, densities) changes when points are dropped. ::: :::: ## Other `geom_*` functions

- [Function reference](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/) — every geom with pictures - [Aesthetic specifications](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html) — every `shape` number, `linetype` name, and color
::: fragment You'll google `ggplot geom` + what you want to draw (or ask Claude). :::
::: fragment There is also a `stat_*()` family for layers that include on-the-fly statistical transformations. See [here](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/layer_stats.html). ::: ## Setup for next bit

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(counties, aes(x = income, y = rent, color = region)) + geom_point(size = 0.6) + labs( x = "Median household income ($ logged)", y = "Median gross rent ($)", color = NULL ) + scale_x_log10() p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Themes

Complete themes restyle everything at once: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment Try `theme_minimal()`, `theme_bw()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_void()`, etc. and packages like `ggthemes` for more. ::: ## Scale your fonts to the medium

Every complete theme takes `base_size` to scale *all* the text together. Paper figures ≈ 11, but slides need much more: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_minimal(base_size = 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment Foreshadowing: What matters is font size _relative to the figure_. Save the same plot smaller and every label looks bigger. ::: ## Or size each piece separately
`theme()` targets one element at a time. Elements take an `element_*()`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + theme( axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold"), axis.text = element_text(size = 10), legend.text = element_text(size = 12, family = "Palatino") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## The `element_*()` family
- `element_text()`, `element_line()` - `element_rect()` — backgrounds and borders - `element_blank()` — removes the element ::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: ::: fragment ::: blocktext A complete theme *resets everything before it*. ::: ::: ## Color palettes

Pick non-default colors or it looks like you didn't try. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + scale_color_viridis_d() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment `viridis` is colorblind-safe and printer-safe. `scale_*_brewer()` uses [ColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org). There are many packages (`paletteer`, `MetBrewer`, etc) ::: ## Or make your own

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pal <- c( "Midwest" = "#E87722", "Northeast" = "steelblue", "South" = "firebrick", "West" = "#83876F" ) p + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + scale_color_manual(values = pal) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Composing figures: `patchwork`

A package can define `+`, `|`, and `/` on `ggplot` objects: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(patchwork) p <- p + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) box <- ggplot(counties, aes(x = region, y = income)) + geom_boxplot() + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) p + box ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## `patchwork` layouts

`|` puts plots beside each other; `/` stacks them: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hist_inc <- ggplot(counties, aes(x = income)) + theme_minimal(base_size = 15) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) (p | box) / hist_inc ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-33-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: fragment What's wrong here? ::: # Publication-ready figures ## Figures are programmatic outputs

Your figures are *products of your code*, same as your tables and estimates ::: fragment - Rerun the script, get the figure without clicking through export UI boxes - Change the data and every figure updates :::
:::: fragment ::: blocktext Never screenshot a plot. If a figure matters enough to share, save it properly at full resolution using code you can rerun. ::: :::: ## Saving plots properly with `ggsave()`

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave("rent_income.pdf", p, width = 6, height = 4) ``` ::: ::: fragment `ggsave()` infers the format from the extension; `width`/`height` are in inches (change with `units` arg). :::
::: fragment Tip: Set `width`/`height` to the actual size in your document and the figures will be proportioned correctly. :::
::: fragment For base R plots the equivalent is: `pdf("fig.pdf", width = 6, height = 4)`, plot, then `dev.off()` ::: ## Vector > raster

| | Formats | What's stored | Zoom in and... | |:-----------|:--------------------|:-----------------|:----------------------| | **Vector** | `pdf`, `svg`, `eps` | shapes and text | stays perfectly crisp | | **Raster** | `png`, `jpg` | a grid of pixels | gets blurry |
::: fragment Use vector formats whenever you can: LaTeX and Word take `pdf`; the web takes `svg` ::: ::: fragment When you're *forced* to raster (some journals, slides software), set `dpi = 300` or more in `ggsave()` ::: # Maps ## Maps are just plots

The `sf` package reads geographic files and gives each row a `geometry` column: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(sf) shapes <- st_read("county_shapes.geojson") ``` :::
::: fragment It looks like a data frame with a special column: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(shapes, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple feature collection with 3 features and 3 fields Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 80165.29 ymin: 60653.63 xmax: 1717985 ymax: 527895.3 Projected CRS: USA_Contiguous_Albers_Equal_Area_Conic GEOID state county geometry 1 18087 Indiana LaGrange County MULTIPOLYGON (((851901.1 52... 2 20107 Kansas Linn County MULTIPOLYGON (((80824.31 10... 3 24029 Maryland Kent County MULTIPOLYGON (((1689187 389... ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Maps, the ggplot way

First attach our county numbers to the shapes: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} shapes_data <- shapes |> left_join( counties |> select(GEOID, income, rent), join_by(GEOID) ) head(shapes_data, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple feature collection with 3 features and 5 fields Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 80165.29 ymin: 60653.63 xmax: 1717985 ymax: 527895.3 Projected CRS: USA_Contiguous_Albers_Equal_Area_Conic GEOID state county income rent geometry 1 18087 Indiana LaGrange County 83741 816 MULTIPOLYGON (((851901.1 52... 2 20107 Kansas Linn County 59200 682 MULTIPOLYGON (((80824.31 10... 3 24029 Maryland Kent County 74402 1144 MULTIPOLYGON (((1689187 389... ``` ::: ::: ## Maps, the ggplot way

This could not be easier: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} shapes_data |> ggplot() + geom_sf() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-39-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Maps, the ggplot way

`geom_sf()` is a geom like any other — aesthetics, scales, and themes all apply: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(shapes_data) + geom_sf(aes(fill = income), linewidth = 0.05) + scale_fill_viridis_c( name = "Median income", breaks = c(50000, 100000, 150000), labels = c("$50k", "$100k", "$150k") ) + theme_void(base_size = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-40-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Pivoting for `facet_*()`

To facet by variable, the variables must live in *one* column — `tidyr`'s `pivot_longer()` stacks them: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} long <- shapes_data |> pivot_longer(c(income, rent)) long |> select(county, name, value) |> head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple feature collection with 4 features and 3 fields Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 80165.29 ymin: 60653.63 xmax: 893059.9 ymax: 527895.3 Projected CRS: USA_Contiguous_Albers_Equal_Area_Conic # A tibble: 4 × 4 county name value geometry 1 LaGrange County income 83741 (((851901.1 523582.1, 855179.6 497385.5, 89305… 2 LaGrange County rent 816 (((851901.1 523582.1, 855179.6 497385.5, 89305… 3 Linn County income 59200 (((80824.31 100142.8, 80165.29 60653.63, 12048… 4 Linn County rent 682 (((80824.31 100142.8, 80165.29 60653.63, 12048… ``` ::: ::: ## Multiple maps

Income dollars dwarf rent dollars, so give each variable its own percentiles, then facet: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} long <- long |> group_by(name) |> mutate(percentile = percent_rank(value)) ggplot(long) + geom_sf(aes(fill = percentile), linewidth = 0.02) + scale_fill_viridis_c() + facet_wrap(~name) + theme_void(base_size = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.png){fig-align='center' width=1344} ::: ::: ## For spatial data, resolution matters

Boundary files often store more detail than we can see. Use `st_simplify()` for plot files if necessary: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # this renders weirdly sometimes: rough <- st_simplify(shapes, dTolerance = 25000, preserveTopology = T) ``` :::
::: fragment Ours is pre-simplified (1.8 MB); raw Census files run much larger and image files will be too large -- and view rendering will take too long. :::
::: fragment The `tigris` package (USA) has `cb` and `resolution` arguments for this. ::: ## This afternoon

- Version control with git and GitHub - Distributions and random draws - Big exercise: a version-controlled, simulated analysis — start to finish
[princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp)
## Now: plotting exercise

Open the exercise: [princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/notes/day-3-viz-ex.pdf](https://princeton-ddss.github.io/r-bootcamp/notes/day-3-viz-ex.pdf)
- A Quarto report with empty chunks — fill them in and render as you go - Everything you need is from this morning # More fun with base R ## Lines: `type = "l"`

All 3,135 counties sorted by income: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(sort(counties$income), type = "l") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-44-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment *What does the rightmost tail tell you?* ::: ## Histograms

A better way to visualize the distribution of one variable (binned): ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hist(counties$income, breaks = 50) ## number of bins ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-45-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Bar plots: counting categories

Use `barplot()` for categorical variables: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} table(counties$region) |> barplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-46-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment (Categories appear alphabetically by default.) ::: ## Densities: a smooth histogram

`density()` estimates the distribution; `plot()` draws the estimate: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} density(counties$income, na.rm = TRUE) |> plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-47-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Densities can smooth *past* data: misleading

::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} d <- density(counties$income, na.rm = TRUE) range(counties$income, na.rm = TRUE) range(d$x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 25425 178707 [1] 17899.87 186232.13 ``` ::: :::
::: fragment The curve starts ~$7,000 below the poorest county. Density estimates commonly leak below zero. ::: ::: fragment The `cut` argument controls this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} d0 <- density(counties$income, na.rm = TRUE, cut = 0) range(d0$x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 25425 178707 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Base R plotting is a canvas

`plot()` (or `hist()`, `barplot()`, ...) starts a **fresh canvas** ::: fragment Then each of these adds ink **on top** of whatever is there: - `points()` — more points - `lines()` — more lines - `abline()` — straight reference lines - `legend()` — add a legend :::
:::: fragment ::: blocktext The canvas is *cumulative*. To change something underneath, start over. ::: :::: ## Layer by layer

Start the canvas — every county in gray: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} nj <- counties[counties$state == "New Jersey", ] plot(counties$income, counties$rent, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = "gray") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-50-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Layer by layer

The canvas is live. Add `points()` on top: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} points(nj$income, nj$rent, pch = 19, col = "orange") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-51-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Layer by layer

...and `abline()` draw a reference line: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} abline(h = median(counties$rent, na.rm = TRUE), lwd = 2, col = "steelblue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-52-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment *Every* New Jersey county sits above the national median rent ::: ## Always label your layers

The same trick compares distributions — start with the Northeast: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(density(counties$income[counties$region == "Northeast"], na.rm = TRUE), col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, main = "Income by region" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-53-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Always label your layers

`lines()` overlays the South: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lines(density(counties$income[counties$region == "South"], na.rm = TRUE), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-54-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment We had to know ahead of time to set ylim. Otherwise we'd have to start over. A pain that `ggplot2` will solve. ::: ## Always label your layers

`legend()` for a legend: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} legend("topright", legend = c("Northeast", "South"), col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-55-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## Many plots at once: `par()`

`par()` sets graphics options for the whole device — `mfrow` makes a grid that fills plot by plot: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) hist(counties$income, main = "Income") hist(counties$rent, main = "Rent") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-56-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ## `par()` is global

Every plot from now on lands in that grid until you put it back: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) ``` :::
::: fragment `par()` controls dozens more settings: margins (`mar` and `oma`), text size (`cex`), etc. :::
:::: fragment ::: blocktext Base R plots are *side effects* that depend on the state of the graphics device. The functions return `NULL`. ::: :::: ## Maps are just plots

`plot()` knows what to do with a geometry column: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} st_geometry(shapes) |> plot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-59-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: fragment What happens if you just call `plot(shapes)`? ::: ## State colors

::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(shapes["state"], main = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-60-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: ::: ## Counties to states

::: fragment ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} shapes |> group_by(state) |> summarise(geometry = st_union(geometry)) |> plot(main = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](day-3-viz_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-61-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768} ::: ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
